newsitem.title: UK: Latvia overcomes banking crisis, sees positive GDP.
newsitem.headline: Latvia overcomes banking crisis, sees positive GDP.

text.p: Latvia has overcome its banking crisis and looks forward to positive GDP growth and a balanced budget in 1997, the country's deputy central bank governor Ilmars Rimsevics said on Thursday .

"We have completely overcome the banking crisis and there is evidence to show that real assets, real capital profits are growing so that the core banking system is completely solid. There are no doubts about that," he told Reuters Financial Television in an interview to be broadcast during an emerging markets briefing.

Latvia was hit by one of the worst banking crises in eastern Europe in 1995. GDP fell 1.6 percent last year amid a credit crunch provoked by the crisis, while its budget deficit swelled to 90 million lats (around $180 million) -- more than double the planned amount.
But the central bank has increased its control over the banking sector and the government has gradually revived the overall economy.

"The banking supervision system in Latvia is considered one of the toughest in Europe," Rimsevics said, citing regular audits not only by the central bank's own examiners but by six big international auditing firms.
"All of this gives us a certain level of comfort so that there is no such trouble on the horizon," he said.
On a three-day visit to London to meet foreign investors, he forecast a turnaround in gross domestic product and lower inflation next year.
"Growth for this year looks around 2 to 3 percent which is quite high considering that last year the GDP growth was minus 1.6 percent," he said.
"First and second quarter growth (this year) was around 2.3 percent which gives us a chance to believe that we can achieve that goal."
He said the government was committed to eliminating the budget deficit by 1997.
"There is a budget almost prepared which shows that 1997 shouldn't have any budget deficit," he said, adding the proposals would go before parliament in early October.
"There is a strong commitment from the government to have a 1997 budget without a deficit," he added.
He forecast 1996 inflation at below 20 percent and lower still next year.

"It will be around 16 or 17 percent (this year) and unless something very unexpected happens with tarrifs, taxes or some other regulations, we hope to achieve a level of 12 percent for next year," Rimsevics said.
Privatisation was steaming ahead, with share listings planned for the country's shipping and gas companies.

"Our privatisation is at full speed and our biggest enterprises are in line to be privatised -- this is one of the most crucial tasks for us," he said, adding the privatisation agencies were preparing to launch a share listing on the Riga stock exchange. --Caroline Brothers, London Newsroom +44 171 542 2734
